name: Non-Contrast Computed Tomography
description: Non-contrast computed tomography scanning (CT scans) is a type of X-ray imaging technique that is used to diagnosis and locate first and recurrent subarachnoid hemorrhage (rebleeding).
description_reference: van Gijn J, and van Dongen KJ. Computed Tomography in the Diagnosis of Subarachnoid Haemorrhage and Ruptured Aneurysm. Clinical Neurology and Neurosurgery, 1980; 82: 11–24. https://doi.org/10.1016/0303-8467(80)90055-4
domain_match_overall_rationale: Directly visualizes new/enlarged intracranial hemorrhage when compared with an earlier scan, which supports the consensus definition of a distinct second bleeding event. In the extracted studies, NCCT demonstrated rebleeding in 19/21 cases (van Gijn, 1980) and 10/12 cases (Tsementzis, 1985). However, not every event was detected, attribution to aneurysm rupture may require clinical/vascular context, and no common rebleeding-specific scoring threshold, standardized imaging interval, or specificity estimate was established.
feasibility_overall_rationale: NCCT is relatively rapid and routinely available in hospital emergency/neurosurgical care and can be compared with baseline scans. Burden includes ionizing radiation, possible repeat exposure, and transport of unstable patients. Scanner access, trained interpretation, and costs vary across intended research settings. NCCT itself does not require contrast. DB = Relatively limited in its application for occlusion as the vasculature is not readily displayed. The strength of CT comes in the assessment of re-bleeding and is probably the first line. While neurological and ICP changes are effective, there can be other reasons for neurological and ICP changes. From clinical experience, I think NCCT offers the quickest way to detect rebleed even if it does not have as much detail as MRI for example. While I agree that transporting a patient to CT may be a challenge, it is certainly not greater than for MRI. I would argue on this basis alone, CT will likely be considered "green" even if it may not perfectively match the domains.

name: Magnetic Resonance Imaging
description: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is an imaging technique that uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves to produce detailed images of the brain. Following aSAH, MRI can be used to identify the presence, location, and extent of new or recurrent bleeding.
domain_match_overall_rationale: MRI can detect acute and subacute intracranial hemorrhage and may be useful in assessing suspected rebleeding. However, identifying a distinct second aneurysmal bleed requires comparison with previous imaging and consideration of other possible causes. The studies cited by the Working Group support MRI for detecting SAH generally, rather than rebleeding specifically, and no study directly evaluating MRI for rebleeding was included in the scoping review. Sequences and criteria used to identify a new bleed need to be clarified.
feasibility_overall_rationale: MRI is available in many tertiary centres and can be useful for assessing intracranial hemorrhage, particularly in selected stable patients. However, its use in suspected rebleeding may be limited by scan duration, availability, transport requirements, motion artefacts, and the need for MRI-compatible monitoring equipment. These concerns are especially relevant for neurologically unstable patients. Overall, I would rate feasibility as Amber, although MRI may be less suitable as the primary method for detecting rebleeding in an emergency. DB = Agreed, I cannot think of any time MRI was first line in the case of rebleeding if it is significant (i.e. on an emergency basis). I suspect MRI will be listed as second line after clinical changes and CT because then you may be able to detect small quantities of blood on FLAIR or SWI/GRE that are otherwise not seen on CT.

name: Clinical Assessment
description: Clinical assessment involves monitoring a patient for changes on a neurological examination, such as a sudden decrease in level of consciousness, new weakness, or speech difficulties. A sudden rise in intracranial pressure may also raise concern for rebleeding. These clinical changes can help signal that rebleeding or another problem may have occured, but imaging is usually needed to confirm the cause.
domain_match_1_rationale: Clinical assessments (Neurological exam or intracranial pressure changes) might suggest rebleeding, but do not necessarily mean a new bleed has occurred. They’re more like warning signs that would lead to further investigation.
feasibility_overall_rationale: Bedside neurological examination is quick, non-invasive, and inexpensive when patients can be examined. Continuous ICP measurement is possible only if a monitor/drain is present or inserted; placement adds burden/risk, equipment, monitoring, staff expertise, and cost. Feasibility differs so much between these approaches that a single combined rating is provisional. Practicality of monitoring does not establish diagnostic specificity for rebleeding.

name: Cerebrospinal Fluid Spectrophotometry
status_rationale: CSF spectrophotometry can not distinguish the initial aSAH event from a distinct second instance of rebleeding. Working Group Leads level of agreement: 100 % (3/3).
description: CSF spectrophotometry is a quantitative method used to measure and follow xanthochromia (the yellow-pigmented cerebrospinal fluid that follows a subarachnoid hemorrhage). It provides a sensitive index that helps clinicians diagnose a subarachnoid hemorrhage and differentiate it from a traumatic lumbar puncture.
description_reference: Tsementzis SA, Hitchcock ER, DeCothi A, et al. Comparative Studies of the Diagnostic Value of Cerebrospinal Fluid Spectrophotometry and Computed Tomographic Scanning in Subarachnoid Hemorrhage. Neurosurgery 1985; 17: 908–12. https://doi.org/10.1227/00006123-198512000-00007

name: Convolutional Neural Networks
status_rationale: Convolution Neural Networks are not commonly available across treatment centres worldwide. Working Group Leads level of agreement: 100 % (3/3).
description: A convolutional neural network is an AI tool trained to identify bleeding on medical scans. It highlights areas that may contain blood and can help clinicians detect, locate, and classify hemorrhage.
description_reference: Barros RS, van der Steen WE, Boers AMM, et al. Automated Segmentation of Subarachnoid Hemorrhages with Convolutional Neural Networks. Informatics in Medicine Unlocked 2020; 19. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.imu.2020.100321
